newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamists strike new conciliatory note.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamists strike new conciliatory note.

text.p: Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, his recent populist trial balloons showing every sign of blowing up in his face, has toned down his rhetoric and drawn closer to his secularist coalition partner.
A series of symbolic Islam-based proposals have apparently been allowed to founder over the Eid al-Fitr holiday, beginning on Sunday to mark the end of the holy month of Ramadan.
Instead, Erbakan has struck a conciliatory note, free of the recent radical Isamist rhetoric that had so alarmed his secularist critics in the army and the opposition parties:

"The adoption of the secular state which has been a turning point in the rise of the Republic on new foundations has enabled the reconciliation of religious freedom in our country with a pluralist, political democracy," he said last week to mark the founding of Turkey's secular system.
A message to the nation on Sunday, celebrating the end of Ramadan, also praised Turkey's pluralistic democracy.

Even those sympathetic to Erbakan have acknowledged that his bid launched during the holy fasting month to instil elements of his Islamist Just Order campaign on secular Turkey was ill-timed, at best.
"What has happened is the last 10 days?" asked the moderate Islamist daily Zaman. "The answer is simple: Erbakan did not understand the dimension of things he spread in public."

The most likely result of this miscalculaton, say analysts and commentators, is a change of tactics to eschew Islamist populism and ensure Welfare's grip on power, in order establish deep party roots within the big state apparatus.
That means restoring ties to his secularist coalition partner Tansu Ciller, whose True Path Party has been upset by Erbakan's recent efforts to satisfy his own radical grassroots.

"What is important today for Welfare are not symbolic gestures like limiting civil servants' hours during Ramadan or wearing of the Islamic headscarf," said political analyst Bilal Cetin on the eve of the Eid, which runs through February 11.

"Now what is important for him is to make use of the opportunity of coming to power...and to stay as long as possible to put down roots in the bureaucracy and in the state," Cetin wrote in the liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil.

The Islamists last month risked the wrath of the secularist armed forces and provoked the opposition with bids to lift a ban on female civil servants wearing the Islamic headscarf and easing bureaucrats' compliance with Ramadan obligations.

Other proposals included the construction of big mosques in traditionally secular neighbourhoods, including the former Christian quarter of Ottoman Istanbul, and building a superhighway to the Moslem holy city of Mecca.
The army last week reminded Erbakan of its secularist vocation, sending a small armoured column through an Islamist stronghold near the capital Ankara.
Citing threats to secularism as enshrined in the Turkish constitution, opposition MPs filed a pair of censure motions that could end the government.

The resulting pressure has forced Welfare and Ciller's True Path Party to embrace each other, despite the wide differences in their views on religion and the state. The two command a slender majority of 279 seats in the 550-member parliament.
Turkish newspapers and television showed the smiling pair breaking the fast at a traditional "iftar" meal, with Ciller proclaiming the coalition's continued health.
"This union of ours will be able to continue for the period of the coalition protocol, we say (the year) 2000, but a long time and maybe beyond that," she told reporters.
Parliament is expected to debate the two censure motions, effectively no-confidence motions, on February 25.
A third such motion is expected from the main opposition Motherland Party one week later. Any one could end Erbakan's tenure as modern Turkey's first Islamist leader.
